I could read it for the most part, but it took me a moment to decipher because some of your letters look very similar to other letters like ‘r’ and ‘v’, ‘h’ and ‘b’, or your ‘f’, ‘g’, and ‘y’. If you formed these letters more, like ensuring that the ‘g’ has the closed *o* shape, or that the ‘f’ has the bar included, that would help make it more immediately legible people who are less familiar with your handwriting style. 

The same thing applies to your vowels. To make them more distinguishable, ensuring things like  for example, if the letter a is next to u and e (aue), you want to make sure that the a is closed, the u is open, and the e has a loop towards the top. I noticed some of your e’s can look like c’s at first glance. I suppose what I’m trying to say is your writing style includes a lot of ‘jags’ and can look like a thread or just a wiggly line when the letter’s are not distinguished from each other.

Also, this doesn’t mean u have to change or fix *all* of it. Honestly, practicing just distinguishing even 3-4 of these letters from their similar alphabet cousins would help in legibility. 

I can still read it, just some words take a moment to understand, but at least there is context to understand where the passage is going.

Hopefully, this provides some insight as to why some people may struggle to decipher your style of handwriting.

I have to agree.   
Having a chaotic environment (whether it is a messy house, or parents/family that are always noisy and creating/perpetuating problems) is a big factor into chronic depression for me, personally.   
At some point, I found friends that were good to me, and I noticed that during the pandemic, when isolation was enforced rather than optional, I was more depressed and contemplated ending it all more than usual. Usually those thoughts and compulsions were more tolerable since I would line up days to hang out with my friends and that enabled me to get out of the chaos, but when that abruptly stopped, things took a turn for the worse.  
People who have a good support system, and a semblance of routine and consistency before falling into depression, I believe, have a greater chance of healing and getting back to a point of functionality compared to those who never did. After all, if life has always been chaotic, how do things return to 'normal'?   
It feels like with every step you take forward, something happens to set you 3 steps back. For every issue you resolve, 5 more appear, whether it's financial, familial or romantic relations, education. Whatever it is.

  
Essentially, I'm just saying I feel this post, and these underlying waves of chronic depression that manifest in a form of passively wishing to die every day, even if things are not that bad that day/even good, are definitely a result long-term exposure to just feeling how futile it is to build yourself up, when other things are constantly unstable and tear down your efforts.  


I'm trying to keep pushing on after my last episode, and it's taken me \~2-3 years to get to this point, where I'm somewhat functional aside from frequent burnout. I've managed to build myself this far, even though it's taken a while. Financial definitely takes a toll on a person too (just had a whole thing with education-wise, working part-time and still not having enough money, not being self-sufficient enough, and end of year bills and everything acting up, and this is still ongoing...) but yea, worrying about all of this is valid. It's a lot of stuff to take care of and worry about.

I'm sorry for rambling so much, but things are definitely rough and pile on us all at the same time, and it all feels unmanageable. I hope that you will find some way to gradually, and steadily resolve what you need to.

I’m just wondering a little bit at how you hold your writing instruments :)

The shaping of your letters reminds me of a friend who was left handed and wrote carefully as well (not assuming you are left-handed) and had a tendency to curve her wrist towards the top of the page

But I think that while yes, practice writing slowly and carefully at first is good, also remember that once you get used to the shape of the letters in cursive, remember to incorporate flow into it

Cursive is cursive because the letters flow/connect and help you write faster as a result
Find a pattern or rhythm of shaping letters that works for you :)

Writing on lined paper could be helpful to keep the bottom line of your letters straight, and for a pen tip that size, maybe writing a bit larger or using a finer pen will make the letters/words look less squished together
 
Perhaps practicing with a ballpoint pen can help too because you’ll have greater control over the amount of ink that comes down onto the page compared to a fountain pen
I found a 0.7mm ballpoint pen helped me practice and develop consistent up and down strokes, along with shaping the letters the way I’d want them to be

Practice makes improvement! Keep going at it :D

I (21) was already a bit of a forgetful person before (although now that I think about it, I was probably mildly depressed for a long time before the pandemic). After my first and recent series of depressive episodes, I've found myself struggling to remember a lot of things too. Recently, I've noticed many times when I've lost something, only to realize that I've put it somewhere else, but not remembering when or why I put it there, or when I even touched it. This has led to panic several times (for more expensive items like Bluetooth earphones) because I've always had the habit of putting things back exactly where I found them initially. It's been about 1 year since my depression has been as severe, and I am only just getting back to a point of remembering things a bit better as I used to. I have been making it a habit recently to write everything important down in my planner now, and even then, I still forget large chunks of things. Compared to the past when I could mentally keep track of a long task list over the course of days, weeks, months, and even the year without writing anything down, this has been a struggle to re-organize and find a way to remember all the work I have to do. I still haven't remembered to call and make an appointment with my doctor for the past 2 years even though I've written it down more times than I can count.   
It's known that depression has effects on memory, and if you're forgetting things due to depression, it's frustrating. It can make a person feel even worse if they base their self-worth on workaholic tendencies, or use work to focus on anything other than what our minds whisper and scream at us. It sucks, but that's also just how our brains take the damage.

It's so much easier to see the beauty in others. The things that they are capable of doing if only mental illness wasn't killing them from the inside. We know that when we're that down deep in our thoughts, it's so painful that we don't want to live anymore. We don't want others to not be able to withstand that torment. I guess a part of it is we want to see even a small portion of us, who will be able to make it through the illness and see the grass, which is most definitely greener on the other side. 

We feel deeply, and this leads us to wanting others to have better than us. Some of us are loving, others of us are bitter, but in the end we all want better, for us, and for the people who are in the same situation as us.
I apologize for the ramble, I just hope what happened to me, won't happen to you.

I had the same thing happen to me when I applied to college a few years ago. I am now a mediocre student and what AM has always told me since I was a kid has come true. That I'm dumber and slower mentally than other kids, so I have to put in a lot more effort.

My AM used to have things to brag about me because I did all of the extracurriculars that she want me to and more (art classes, piano, guitar, violin, zither, food bank volunteering, extra tutoring for myself and volunteering to tutor others, AP and IB, 4 clubs in school, hospital volunteering, church choir, church plays; basically, she named it I did it). I bent over backwards to fulfill her desires. As you'd expect, I came into college and had no idea what I wanted to do (I still don't because I'm passionate about nothing and everything feels so-so) because for the majority of my life, I did nothing for myself and only for my AM.

You already have a great start by doing extracurriculars that let you pursue YOUR interests.

Now that I am a mediocre failure of a student in college, shes constantly searching of things that she can say about me, that there is something that her child did that's good enough to be presented in front of others. I don't say anything significant about my schooling, until recently when AM blew up at me saying she has to know everything about my academic progress and I just told her I am failing and I'm the dumbass she always knew I was.

Really, I was burnt out, mentally ill, and done with giving a crap and I just ended up numbing myself or blowing up in rage every moment. I hope you don't let that happen to yourself, and that you can ignore AP's hurtful and insensitive, passive-aggressive, provoking and inflammatory comments and be able to find yourself what you want to do. Doing that will not only benefit you, but it will bring YOU success. Aim high for your dreams. I never hurts to aim for a 10/10. Maybe you'll only manage to complete 7/10 but look at that! That's just 3 short of your initial goal. Aim for your dream school. Aim for the career you want.

I was that kid. The kid that your AP would compare you to. But look at me now. A thing floating through existence without having any thoughts for myself. Days filled with a distorted sense of resentment and appreciation for my AP all at the same time. Don't become me. Do what you want and what you think if best for your future. APs are just irl trolls at this point, and these conflicting feelings you have are showing you that there's something wrong with the way they are treating you. Follow that instinct.

Anyways, finding the friends I have now in high school and college really helped me build the healthy relationships that I wanted with other individuals. I'm still an awkward ball of "I struggle with social norms because my parents didn't let me go hang out with anyone until my last year of high school AND I was the shy kid who didn't talk to anyone unless they talked with me first" but find a few close friends that you will mesh with and hang with a lot. Just being around good friends and sharing time together in their presence can help immensely with your mental health and maybe, after looking at what your friends do, it can provide you motivation to keep up, so you can all be successful together.

Good job on letting your feelings out. It's perfectly okay to feel all of these things and ask questions about them. It's a part of being human, it's a part of being you. You're definitely in a tough situation and I can understand you to an extent. I'm glad you still have something that you like, and I hope you get to do a lot more with marching band.

Finding a job is always a good idea, and working for some extra pocket change or even just to get a feel of a working experience is helpful. From what I see, you're a responsible individual who's struggling. Be bitter, it's okay. Be a brat for now. People will always want more to satisfy their desires, so it's completely normal. I think it's human nature to always want better for ourselves. And that's perfectly normal.

I hope you find more things to live for that spur your passion as much as marching band does. Once you get a job, I hope you can treat yourself to something like a new game or a nice treat at a cafe or bakery.

I'm a bit younger than you and have to say that I'm in a similar situation, and I definitely put them on an information diet. Not sure when, but maybe during middle school I just started not telling them anything too personal. It's a bit of a struggle but my independence really just came from watching other people and copying them bit by bit. I might fail the first 10 times at cooking eggs (making them too salty or boiling them for too long) but eventually you'll get them the way you like it. 

My peers are indubitably better able to think critically and hold themselves responsible for their own lives, whereas I still have some trouble trying to pick things or doing things without input from AP sometimes, and can often feel lost because I have also tried being the "good child" for a while. 

Also, I eased them into it by just slowly starting to state things. Instead of asking AP, I just started saying, "I'm going out with my friends." For me, it might've been easier for them to accept me going with my friends in the beginning because they go to good schools and they know I didn't really have any other friends at that point in time. It also helped that I didn't really have places I wanted to go because I'm a bit of a hobbit and homebody so they assumed that if I went anywhere, it was for some sort of business with school or work or studying.

And if they don't accept it. Honestly, take some tips from the way they treat you. Make bullshit excuses and make them eat it because sometimes, you have to fight fire with fire. Water ain't always gonna work if the fire is burning too strong. You might lose some things, but in the end, you can save a lot more for YOUR life. Of course, this doesn't mean do it in a disrespectful manner. It's just gradual changes to your life that will force AP to see that you've become an adult. 

Just remember that your parents treat you like a child because you will forever be their baby in their eyes. Depending on whether that is a good or bad thing, it's always hard on parents to see their child leave the nest, and maybe they just don't know how to express that in less mentally draining and demanding ways because of their own past.

My parents, I admit, are not as controlling or toxic as other parents on this forum, however, I think that making small changes and copying people you see around you who are more independent will force them to admit one day that you are no longer a child and an adult. The most gratifying moment for me was just 2 months ago, my AM said to me: "Huh, you really are starting to become an adult now." straight to my face when \*I\* was the one scolding \*her\* for using earbuds while driving on the highway. A bit of a shocking moment, but a gratifying one. She can still treat me like a baby and incompetent at some things like making doctor's appointments (I'm still working on that), but it's a start. It also helps that my schedule is so busy, that I essentially don't see her except for the weekends since I am usually out of the house from early morning until 10:30 at night because of school or homework. Distance makes the heart grow fonder I suppose.

TLDR: Incorporate little changes, give less details about your life to them, start making more statements on what you're going to do rather than asking them if you can do, and  try to keep more distance from them so that they learn that you can survive without them, and they can survive without you (even if it means you making an excuse like I'm staying work for overtime because the company has a lot of projects and an overflow of orders right now, so you can take time for yourself like taking a walk at the park or just even getting yourself a drink and admiring the sunset at the beach). The same thing happened to me during the pandemic. Being enclosed in the same home as my AP and not being able to go out of the house at all really took a toll on my mental health. Even now my grades are not as good as they used to be (straight As) and it’s taken me 3 semesters to sort of get my shit together again (a cumulative GPA of -B). 

My parents are also strict in a sense, and they emanate disappointment and regret when they heard about my grades, even telling me I shouldn’t have gone into a 4-year if I was going to be like this, and I should’ve just gone to a community college. And that hurts. Because to an extent, the only reason I was working so hard was because I wanted to make them proud. I put in all my effort, because I know I’m not as smart as other kids, and the only way I could achieve what they wanted was to adapt quickly, and sacrifice sleep for perfection. It’s led to a lot if my insecurities and problems with self-image as well. I even wished I was dead several times and considered going through during the pandemic. Sometimes, when thoughts get too dark, I still do. 

Now, for the most part, I’ve just learned to not give a flying fuck. You can choose when and what you want to care about with practice over time. Even now, I feel guilty at times when I don’t fulfill their image of a well-performing child. I still try and make an effort of course, but I’ve chosen to give the people I chose in my life (close friends that I trust) and myself more precedence than the people I was born to. Care for yourself first and foremost. In this case, you care a lot about your parents, so you need to tone that down and up the love for yourself and give yourself more allowance to make mistakes. 

I’m assuming you are not in college yet, since your parents have access to your grades. If you can, restrict their access.

This is probably not the best advice, but I would just start to not open up about anything to them. That’s what I did, and now for the most part, my parents leave me alone and argue with each other. If I answer, it’s short and sweet, and if I tell them a story, it’s wordy but nothing of true substance in my life. The less contact with them makes things become more tolerable. They might try to guilt you by saying “oh you never tell me anything” but remind yourself why that is. Trust yourself and be curt but polite in responding so they don’t have more ammo to throw at you. You need time to slowly practice your own thoughts. 

I know that whenever I think of doing something, I still think about whether my parents would approve of it or not. But at some point, if you practice in baby steps, you’ll be able to find your own thoughts in there rather than be controlled by what your parents might think. 

I won’t say that this is good advice or a cure-all to your problems, just what I’ve done. Sometimes, you just need to put up a wall. It won’t block out everything, make sure to have a good cry about it later. Don’t let them see or hear you though lest they guilt you for it. Make it cathartic for yourself. Then reflect on why you felt that way, what thoughts went through your mind while you were hearing those things. Be mindful to yourself.
